lessons.title: Lesson 1: Coaching and mentoring: what is the difference?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Choose whether a situation calls for coaching, mentoring or simply telling.
This lesson builds toward: Given a situation where someone needs help, you will choose whether it calls for coaching, mentoring or telling, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
Coaching helps a person find their own answers through questions and listening. The coach does not need to know the job better; the person being coached does most of the thinking. It works well when someone has the skill or knowledge but is stuck, or needs to grow their judgment.
Mentoring is a longer relationship where someone with more experience shares advice, stories, contacts and lessons learned. A mentor often works in the same field. It works well for career choices, learning "how things really work" and building a network.
Sometimes neither is right and you should just tell. A new worker about to make a safety mistake needs instruction, not questions. Good leaders switch between telling, coaching and mentoring depending on what the person needs.
Words to know:
- Coaching: helping someone find their own answers by asking questions and listening.
- Mentoring: a longer relationship where someone more experienced shares advice and lessons.
- Mentee: the person being mentored.
- Coachee: the person being coached.
Try it now: Write three real situations from your work or life where someone asked you for help. For each, write whether coaching, mentoring or telling would help most, and why.
You can now tell coaching from mentoring and choose the right approach for a situation.

options: A longer relationship where someone with more experience shares advice and lessons
Asking only yes or no questions
check.why: Mentoring shares experience over time, often in the same field.

check.q: A team member is curious about how promotions really work in your field. Which approach fits best?
options: Tell them to read the policy alone
Mentor them by sharing your experience and contacts
check.why: Mentoring fits career choices and learning how things really work.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Listening so people feel heard
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Listen fully and show you understood by summarizing.
This lesson builds toward: In a conversation, you will listen without interrupting and summarize what you heard, so the person agrees you understood or corrects you.
Most of us listen while planning what we will say next. In coaching, that gets in the way. Full listening means giving all your attention to the other person: phone away, eyes on them, no interrupting, and not jumping in with your own story.
Show you are listening. Nod, say "go on", and every few minutes summarize: "So what I'm hearing is that you want to lead the project but you're worried the team won't follow. Is that right?" A good summary lets the person hear their own thinking and correct you if you got it wrong.
Listen for feelings and values as well as facts: "You sound frustrated" or "It sounds like fairness really matters to you." Get comfortable with silence. A pause often comes just before the person's best idea.
Step by step:
- Put your phone away and face the person.
- Don't interrupt or jump in with your own story.
- Encourage them: nod, "go on".
- Summarize what you heard and ask if it is right.
- Name feelings you notice.
- Allow silence.
Words to know:
- Active listening: listening with full attention and showing you understood, for example by summarizing.
- Summarize: to repeat the main points briefly in your own words.
Try it now: Ask a partner to talk for three minutes about something they want to improve. Don't give advice. Then summarize what you heard in two sentences and ask, "Did I get that right?"
You can now listen with full attention and summarize so the other person feels heard.

check.q: What gets in the way of full listening?
options: Planning what you will say next
check.why: Planning your reply means you are not fully listening.

check.q: While someone talks about a problem, you remember a similar story of your own. What would you do?
options: Keep listening and summarize what they said
check.why: Full listening means not jumping in with your own story.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking powerful questions
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn advice into open questions that help people think for themselves.
This lesson builds toward: When someone asks for your advice, you will ask open questions that start with what or how instead of giving advice, asking at least five open questions in one conversation.
A powerful question is open (it cannot be answered with yes or no), short, and about the other person's thinking. It often starts with "what" or "how": "What would success look like?" "What have you already tried?" "What's really stopping you?"
Watch out for advice dressed up as a question, like "Have you thought about calling her?" That is your idea, not theirs. Also be careful with "why" questions, which can sound like blame. "What led you to that?" usually feels kinder than "Why did you do that?"
One strong question is "And what else?" It helps people go past their first answer. Ask one question at a time, then stop and listen.
Step by step:
- Start with "what" or "how".
- Keep it short and about their thinking.
- Avoid advice dressed up as a question.
- Swap "why" for "what led you to...".
- Ask "And what else?"
- Ask one question, then stop and listen.
Words to know:
- Open question: a question that can't be answered with just yes or no.
- Closed question: a question answered with yes, no or a single fact.
Try it now: Write down three pieces of advice you often give people. Turn each into an open question. For example, "You should ask your boss" becomes "Who could help you with this?"
You can now ask short, open questions that help people find their own answers.

options: It cannot be answered with yes or no
check.why: Open questions invite the person to think and explain.

check.q: You want to suggest your idea, "Talk to your supervisor." How would you turn it into a coaching question?
options: "Have you thought about talking to your supervisor?"
"Why haven't you talked to your supervisor?"
check.why: An open question lets them find the idea; the others are advice or blame.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Running a conversation with the GROW model
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Guide a coaching conversation through Goal, Reality, Options and Will.
This lesson builds toward: In a 20-minute coaching conversation, you will guide the talk through Goal, Reality, Options and Will, ending with a first step, a date and a commitment rating.
GROW is a simple, widely used map for a coaching conversation. G is the Goal: what do they want from this talk and longer term? R is Reality: what is happening now, what have they tried? O is Options: what could they do? W is Will (or Way forward): what will they do, and when?
Spend time on Reality before rushing to Options. Often the person sees the answer once the situation is clear. In Options, ask for several ideas, and "what else?", before choosing. If you have an idea, you can offer it last, as one option among many.
End with a clear commitment: "What's your first step, and when will you do it?" Ask how sure they are on a scale of 1 to 10. If it is low, ask what would make it higher.
Step by step:
- Goal: "What do you want to get out of this talk?"
- Reality: "What's happening now? What have you tried?"
- Options: "What could you do? What else?"
- Will: "What will you do, and by when?"
- Check commitment: "How sure are you, 1 to 10?"
Words to know:
- GROW model: a four-step coaching map: Goal, Reality, Options, Will.
- Commitment: a clear promise to take a specific action by a certain time.
Try it now: Write one GROW question for each step on a card. With a partner, hold a 15-minute GROW conversation about something they want to improve. End with their first step and a date.
You can now guide a coaching conversation from goal to a clear, committed next step with GROW.

check.q: In GROW, what does the O stand for?
check.why: GROW is Goal, Reality, Options, Will.

check.q: Ten minutes in, the person has listed only one option. What would you ask?
check.why: "And what else?" helps people go past their first answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Setting a development goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Help someone turn a wish into a clear, measurable development goal.
This lesson builds toward: Given a wish to grow a skill, you will write a clear development goal with small learning steps, saying what, how much and by when, and owned by the person.
A development goal is about growing a skill, not just finishing a task. "Get better at speaking" is a wish. A clear goal says what, how much and by when: "Lead the Monday team huddle on my own, three weeks in a row, by the end of March."
Many people use SMART to check a goal: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. The person should own the goal. Ask what they want to grow, and why it matters to them, before adding what the job needs.
Break the goal into small learning steps: something to read or watch, someone to watch or shadow, a chance to practice, and someone to give feedback. Most growth comes from doing, not only from courses.
Step by step:
- Ask what they want to grow and why it matters.
- Write it as what, how much, by when.
- Check it with SMART.
- List learning steps: read, watch someone, practice, get feedback.
- Agree the first step.
Words to know:
- Development goal: a goal to grow a skill or ability.
- SMART: a goal check: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
- Shadowing: learning by watching someone do the work.
Try it now: With your practice partner, turn one wish into a SMART development goal. Then list three learning steps, including at least one chance to practice.
You can now help someone write a clear development goal and the learning steps to reach it.

check.q: Which is a wish rather than a clear development goal?
options: "Present the monthly report on my own at two meetings by June"
"Run three safety briefings alone by the end of the quarter"
"Train two new staff on the till by May 1"
check.why: A clear goal says what, how much and by when; a wish does not.

check.q: Your mentee wants to get better at handling upset customers. Which learning step would you add first?
options: Shadow a skilled coworker, then practice with feedback
check.why: Most growth comes from doing and practicing with feedback.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Mentoring agreements and tracking growth
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a simple mentoring agreement and a tracker to follow someone's growth.
This lesson builds toward: When starting a mentoring relationship, you will write a one-paragraph mentoring agreement and a tracker with three check-in dates, covering how often, how, for how long and what is private.
A mentoring relationship works better with a short agreement at the start. Agree on the purpose, how often you will meet (for example monthly for six months), how (in person, phone or video), what is private, who sets the agenda (usually the mentee), and how either person can end it kindly.
Track growth so you both see progress. A simple tracker can be a shared document or spreadsheet with the goal, learning steps, check-in dates, what was tried, what was learned, and the next step. Celebrate progress, even small steps.
At each check-in, look back at the goal, ask what went well and what was hard, and agree the next step. At the end, review together what changed, and talk about what comes next: a new goal, a new mentor, or becoming a mentor yourself.
Step by step:
- Agree purpose, how often, how, and for how long.
- Agree what stays private and who sets the agenda.
- Agree how either person can end it kindly.
- Set up a tracker: goal, steps, dates, learning, next step.
- At each check-in: review, reflect, next step.
- At the end, review what changed and what's next.
Words to know:
- Mentoring agreement: a short written understanding of how a mentoring relationship will work.
- Tracker: a simple record of progress toward a goal, with dates.
- Check-in: a planned meeting to review progress.
Try it now: Final task: hold a 20-minute GROW conversation with your partner. Then write together their SMART development goal, a one-paragraph mentoring agreement, and a tracker with three check-in dates.
You can now set up a mentoring relationship with a clear agreement and track someone's growth over time.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Listening Talked more than the partner or interrupted often. Listened more than they talked and summarized at least once. Named a feeling or value they heard, and the partner agreed. Open questions Fewer than five open questions, or mostly advice. At least five open questions, one at a time. Used "And what else?" and avoided blaming "why" questions. GROW conversation Skipped a step or jumped straight to advice. Covered Goal, Reality, Options and Will and ended with a first step and a date. Asked for a 1 to 10 commitment rating and what would make it higher. Development goal The goal is a wish, such as "get better at speaking". A clear goal that says what, how much and by when, owned by the partner. Broken into small learning steps with practice and feedback. Agreement and tracker The agreement or tracker is missing. A one-paragraph agreement (how often, how, how long, what is private) and a tracker with three check-in dates. Also says how either person can end it kindly. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who usually sets the agenda in a mentoring meeting?
check.why: The mentee usually sets the agenda, since it is their growth.

check.q: At a check-in, your mentee has made a small step forward. What would you do?
options: Celebrate it and agree the next step
check.why: Celebrating small progress keeps people motivated.
